papers.title: Pharmacy stock and post-earthquake access to medicines in Tokyo: modeling choices that change recovery judgments
papers.abstract: Community pharmacies sustain access to medicines after an earthquake only while open, staffed and stocked. Accessibility models rarely represent stock depletion, and the assumptions this requires may change conclusions about recovery. We examine these assumptions for over-the-counter (OTC) medicines supplied by 4,748 registered pharmacies in Tokyo's 23 wards during the first week after a magnitude-7.3 scenario earthquake. A two-step floating catchment area model computes walking accessibility for 2,651 grid cells (500 m) under 10,000 sampled combinations of stock duration, staffing, operation and demand. Results are expressed as Retention: post-disaster accessibility divided by the same cell's pre-disaster accessibility. First, the assumed link between stock and service, the supply a pharmacy can still provide, determines the recovery verdict. If service falls in proportion to remaining stock, mean Retention declines from 0.479 (days 2-3) to 0.273 (days 4-7). If service is maintained until stock falls below one quarter, the mean rises instead, although low-end (10th-percentile) outcomes still decline. Measuring at the start of each period rather than averaging over it also reverses the trend. Second, a simple model that rescales a fixed map by citywide supply and demand reproduces citywide patterns but cannot evaluate where pharmacies close or where capacity is added; a spatial model run once on average inputs can. Third, four floating catchment methods agree on overall rankings (rank correlation 0.81), but their lowest-ranked 10% of cells overlap only partially (Jaccard index 0.56). Disaster assessments should report stock assumptions and low-end outcomes, and treat local priority areas as method-dependent.

papers.title: Triage Accuracy of Jev and Open-Weight System One Decision Models and Their Use for Early Emergency Recognition in Symptom-Assessment Applications
papers.abstract: Laypeople increasingly use large language models (LLMs) for triage advice, but LLMs answer in variable free text, which makes it hard to evaluate them for use in medical devices. Decision models, which assign a probability to each predefined triage category, may be easier to evaluate. To test their triage accuracy, we evaluated 16 decision models (14 open-weight, 2 proprietary) on 233 synthetic and 10,000 real-world cases, yielding 163,728 total assessments. The best models triaged 72.1% of synthetic cases correctly and agreed with an existing algorithm in 56.1% of real-world cases. They were more promising for recognising emergencies early: given only demographics, chief complaints, risk factors and red-flag answers, the best model reached an AUROC of 0.87. At a 5% error margin, it could decide for or against emergencies for about half of users. Decision models should therefore not replace triage engines but could shorten symptom assessments at setting-specific error margins.

papers.title: When AI Performance Is Not Enough: Statistical Guardrails for Clinical Development
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) are reshaping the operational and inferential landscape of clinical development, yet their adoption frequently outpaces the statistical scrutiny these methods demand. This commentary offers first-principles perspectives across four application domains: anomaly detection in clinical trial data, real-time monitoring and adaptive trial designs, biomarker-based enrichment, and virtual and digital twins. For each domain, we articulate the underlying inferential problem, the contribution of AI and ML relative to established statistical methods, and the risks that statisticians, data scientists, and clinical developers must actively manage. Across these domains, a unifying theme emerges: AI and ML methods may succeed locally while failing to satisfy the broader statistical assumptions required for valid clinical and regulatory decisions. These risks include false-positive signals, compromised Type I error control in adaptive designs, conflation of prognostic with predictive biomarkers, and causal claims not supported by data and assumptions. We argue that a clearly defined context of use, relevant statistical assumptions, and consequences of the intended decision should guide the evaluation. For treatment-effect questions, the ICH E9(R1) estimand framework provides a useful organizing principle. Responsible use of AI in clinical development requires not restraint, but rigor: the inferential discipline necessary to make these technologies reproducible, interpretable, and defensible in the service of patients.

papers.title: Inferring behind-the-meter demand components from net load via inverse optimization
papers.abstract: Understanding and forecasting electricity demand responses to price signals is essential to support the operational decisions of system operators, retailers, and regulators. Traditional time series and machine learning approaches have performed well under stable consumption patterns. However, the rise of active consumers with flexible assets, such as solar-plus-storage systems and electric vehicles, introduces new complexities. These consumers exhibit behind-the-meter behavior that is generally unobservable to system operators and retailers, who can typically only measure net demand at the boundary meters which are located at the connection points to the grid. Net demand reflects the aggregate of baseload consumption, flexible load shifting, and self-generation, all of which may respond nonlinearly to market prices. As these unobservable components grow, existing forecasting models may fail to capture the true dynamics of consumer behavior. This work develops and implements a data-driven inverse optimization framework to reveal behind-the-meter consumption patterns using only net demand data. By analyzing net demand as revealed at the grid connection point, we estimate parameters for a latent optimization model, enabling predictions that infer the unobservable components. This enables more accurate point and probabilistic forecasting of electricity demand under varying price signals. Thus, it provides actionable insights for system operators to improve local congestion management and flexibility extraction, as well as for retailers and aggregators, who could thereby optimize operations and tariffs to leverage consumer flexibility. We validate the methodology using real-world data, demonstrating improved forecasting accuracy over leading machine learning and time-series benchmarks.

papers.title: Global Parameter Identification and Uncertainty Quantification of reduced-order ADM1 using Maximum Likelihood Estimation and Bayesian Inference
papers.abstract: Anaerobic digestion (AD) models can be challenging to calibrate against real data due to limited practical identifiability, data scarcity, and model complexity. Weighted least squares objective functions and gradient-based solvers using finite differences are often used in literature, but result in suboptimal parameter estimates and large uncertainty bands. This paper identifies the parameters of a reduced-order ADM1 by comparing the frameworks of maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) and Bayesian inference (BI), and quantifies uncertainties of parameters and outputs. Multirate experimental data are taken from a lab-scale AD reactor fed with agricultural substrates and operated at organic loading rates of 3$\,$g VS $\mathrm{m^{-3}d^{-1}}$. Global optima are found via global and gradient-based local search algorithms using forward sensitivities. Enhanced scatter search provides the best global search results. These are refined by the Gauss-Newton algorithm as the best local search, which delivers $R^2$ values of 0.95 for acetic acid and 0.77 for biogas production. BI yields substantially narrower uncertainty bands than MLE and avoids the need for a global search by incorporating prior knowledge about parameter distributions. The search space is captured efficiently by log10 scaling of parameters. Algorithmic details on its implications are provided. Despite a high-resolution lab-scale dataset, the ADM1-specific inhibition parameter $K_\mathrm{I,nh3}$ is practically not identifiable with MLE, and shows a low output sensitivity, whereas a parameter for the effective ion concentration shows superb practical identifiabilty at high confidence with both MLE and BI. The present work lays a scalable base for calibration of nonlinear AD models by providing reliable simulations. It thus advances model-based monitoring and control applications of multirate processes such as agricultural AD plants.

papers.title: A hybrid Graph-based Machine Learning Model for predicting Delivery Times in Supply Chain Logistics
papers.abstract: Global supply chains are increasingly vulnerable to disruptions arising from external events, such as natural disasters and geopolitical crises, and from internal operational inefficiencies, including supplier delays and bottlenecks in order shipping. This work, conducted within the Horizon Europe project M4ESTRO, introduces a hybrid modelling approach combining graph theory and machine learning to represent supply chain logistics operations, with a focus on predicting delays in inbound flows between industrial suppliers and manufacturing entities. The various stages of order fulfilment are modelled through a formal mathematical framework, by defining disruption indicators computed from both historical and real-time data drawn from heterogeneous sources, including traffic and weather conditions and supplier dispatch readiness. Building on a graph-based representation of the supply chain, stochastic methods based on Markov chains are applied to estimate delivery times, detect schedule deviations, quantify prediction uncertainty, and produce interpretable metrics to support operational decision-making. Within the M4ESTRO project, the proposed framework was applied to build a web application for real-time tracking of inbound logistics, and was validated in a use case with an industrial project partner. The web application successfully enabled early detection of logistics disruptions along the supply chain and provided stakeholders with the visibility needed to act before delays propagated. The underlying model proved effective as the basis of a resilient, data-driven logistics tracking system, aligned with the digital transformation objectives of industry and with Manufacturing-as-a-Service paradigms.

papers.title: Geospatial foundation models and deep learning for climate resilience: a review of transfer, uncertainty and decision readiness
papers.abstract: Geospatial foundation models can reuse information learned from large Earth-observation archives, but their value for climate resilience depends on whether that information transfers to unfamiliar events, regions and observing conditions. This review connects advances in deep learning with the evidence needed for hazard monitoring and early warning. A descriptive audit of 137 full-text hazard-application studies is interpreted alongside a separate corpus of 37 model and benchmark records. Ninety-eight application studies reported an out-of-distribution experiment, whereas headline evaluations included held-out events in 31 studies, regions in 25 and sensors in only two. None of the ten studies coded for geospatial foundation-model fine-tuning used sensor holdout as a headline test. Uncertainty-related methods were recorded in 16 studies, including two with explicitly calibrated probabilistic output. These overlapping counts describe evaluation practice within the coded corpus, not a ranking of model families. We distinguish Earth-observation representation learning from atmospheric forecasting and examine how labels, observability, forecast lead time and decision requirements constrain their contribution across flood, wildfire, drought, heat, cryosphere and cascading-hazard applications. We then develop a decision-backward evaluation framework: define the action and information available when it must be taken, reproduce the relevant shift, retain a matched task-specific baseline, and report misses, false alarms, reliability and end-to-end latency. The framework turns transferability from a broad model claim into a testable requirement for climate adaptation and risk management.

papers.title: Katz Kernel Based Stratification of Breast Cancer Patients
papers.abstract: The integration of mechanistic signaling networks into clinical research has become a cornerstone of precision oncology. By capturing the complex biochemical interactions within a cell, these networks provide a functional map of disease progression that goes beyond simple genomic mutations. Consequently, the development of specific signaling models of patients has significant relevance, allowing for a more granular representation of individual disease profiles. In this setting, there is a growing need for robust methodologies capable of comparing graph based pathway structures to identify similarities and differences across patient cohorts. Such comparisons are essential for the identification of clinically meaningful subgroups, and the discovery of novel biomarkers. Standard graph kernels, while mathematically rigorous, often remain too generic for this purpose. They frequently fail to capture features specific to gene signaling networks, resulting in suboptimal clustering performance. In this paper, we present a domain specific graph kernel designed for mechanistic signaling networks. Unlike generic approaches, our method explicitly incorporates biological constraints and gene interaction patterns into the kernel formulation, enabling a more accurate characterization of both topological structure and functional behavior. We assess its performance on breast cancer datasets, focusing on its ability to support disease subtyping. Our results suggest that our approach can effectively contribute to patient stratification.

papers.title: Religious expression and well-being across countries and regions: Evidence from a decade of social media posts
papers.abstract: This study examines whether social connectedness constitutes a pathway between religious expression and subsequent well-being. Drawing on millions of social-media posts, we combine broad international coverage, subnational geographic detail, and annual observations over 2013-2022 to examine religious expression, connectedness, and three well-being dimensions. The longitudinal models account for baseline connectedness and well-being, geographic and year effects, and national trends. National longitudinal models support positive indirect associations through social connectedness for happiness and life satisfaction. The indirect estimates for purpose nationally and for all three outcomes regionally are positive but imprecise. Complementary coefficient contrasts in contemporaneous regional models and comparisons of regional period averages show stronger associations of religious expression with purpose than with either happiness or life satisfaction. Together, these findings support a national pathway through social connectedness for the affective and evaluative dimensions of well-being. The stronger regional associations with purpose motivate further investigation of meaning- and direction-related processes beyond the measured connectedness pathway.

papers.title: Model-Assisted Probability of Detection Studies for Image-Based Human Inspection
papers.abstract: Establishing a probability of detection (POD) curve is important for assessing the reliability of components in aging systems. Traditional POD studies rely on physical specimens containing representative flaws and human inspectors who record detection results, making such studies costly. This paper demonstrates how appropriately validated physics-based simulation can substantially reduce, and in suitable applications potentially replace, physical POD experiments. We use XRSIM, an X-ray radiographic simulator, to generate weld images containing cracks of varying size, morphology, and location. Flaw characteristics, locations, and the number of flaws per image were randomized, with images containing zero to three flaws. Each simulated flaw is treated as an observational unit contributing flaw-level hit-miss responses. To capture human inspection variability, the images were presented in random order to five inspectors, each of whom inspected the images twice. The resulting data were analyzed using a repeated-measures binary-regression model accounting for flaw-to-flaw, inspector-to-inspector, flaw/inspector-combination, and inspection-to-inspection variability. Bayesian inference was used to estimate the population-mean POD curve, inspector-specific POD curves, and associated statistical uncertainty. Results show that flaw-to-flaw variability dominates, with appreciable differences among inspectors. The study provides a framework for combining physics-based image simulation with controlled human inspection to estimate POD while reducing the experimental burden of physical specimen fabrication.

papers.title: Multilevel non-linear interrupted time series analysis
papers.abstract: Recent advances in interrupted time series analysis permit characterization of a typical non-linear interruption effect through use of generalized additive models. Concurrently, advances in latent time series modeling allow efficient Bayesian multilevel time series models. We propose to combine these concepts with a hierarchical model selection prior to characterize interruption effects with a multilevel structure, encouraging parsimony and partial pooling while incorporating meaningful variability in causal effects across subpopulations of interest, while allowing poststratification. These models are demonstrated with three applications: 1) the effect of the introduction of the prostate specific antigen test on prostate cancer diagnosis rates by race and age group, 2) the change in stroke or trans-ischemic attack hospitalization rates across Medicare beneficiaries by rurality in the months after the start of the COVID-19 pandemic, and 3) the effect of Medicaid expansion in Missouri on the proportion of inpatient hospitalizations discharged with Medicaid as a primary payer by key age groupings and sex.

papers.title: A Calculus Gradient: Child Poverty, Mathematics Preparation, and First-Year College Performance at a Hispanic-Serving University
papers.abstract: The San Antonio metropolitan area has one of the highest poverty rates among large U.S. metropolitan areas. Within Bexar County, where the city is located, child poverty varies widely across school districts. We link entrants of the city's public research university, a broad-access Hispanic-Serving Institution, to their sending schools and districts, and examine their preparation scores and first-year outcomes. Across the nation's school districts, enrollment in widely taken core courses (Algebra II, Geometry, Biology) shows little relation to child poverty, while enrollment in Calculus and Advanced Placement mathematics and science is far lower where child poverty is higher, nationally and within Bexar County. Among linked entrants, mathematics preparation differs with the school and district. Entrants with stronger mathematics preparation earn higher first-year grades in nearly every subject. Most entrants who do not return after the first year had unsuccessful courses, and mathematics is the largest single source of those outcomes. Among students who change major, mathematics is one of the subjects with grades furthest below their own averages. Within the same course and term, larger mathematics sections go with more unsuccessful outcomes for entrants with lower mathematics preparation, which identifies a hypothesis for testing smaller sections. Recorded between Fall 2014 and Fall 2019, these outcomes offer a reference point for change after the pandemic, test-optional admissions, and generative artificial intelligence. The analysis is reproducible; adapting it elsewhere requires local definitions and linkage validation. All results are associations among the students of one institution; establishing causes would require a designed study.

papers.title: Directed Hypergraphs: Tensor Representation, Embedding Modeling, and Community Detection
papers.abstract: Directed hypergraphs, in which each hyperedge connects a set of tail nodes to a set of head nodes, are the natural representation for many-to-many interactions in citation networks, metabolic pathways, and group communications. Despite their broad applicability, community detection for directed hypergraphs remains statistically underdeveloped: most existing methods either collapse hyperedges into pairwise edges, treat the two sides as interchangeable, or require the number of communities to be known. We propose a statistical framework for simultaneous embedding and community detection in nonuniform directed hypergraphs. The method allows each node to have distinct roles as a source and as a target, accommodates varying hyperedge sizes, and automatically determines the unknown numbers of communities on both sides, which need not be equal, through a fusion-penalized likelihood. We establish consistency of the estimated numbers of communities, exact recovery of both membership structures, and consistent probability tensor estimation. We further show that exact recovery is attainable without knowing the numbers of communities by a procedure that does not rely on any particular local solution, and we complement the upper bounds with a minimax lower bound for probability tensor estimation and a necessary condition for exact recovery. To ground the methodology, we construct the Cross-Statistics Citation Network, a new large-scale corpus linking Statistics with Biology, Computer Science, and Economics. Applying our method to this corpus reveals source and target roles of author communities in cross-field knowledge flow, and a pairwise representation of the same citations partly merges these roles.

papers.title: Structural and Lagrangian properties of analogue ensembles to characterize multifractality of stochastic processes
papers.abstract: We present a framework for the scale-invariance characterization of stochastic processes in reconstructed finite-dimensional spaces. This framework analyses the structural and dynamical properties of the reconstructed space and is based on a Takens embedding reconstruction followed by the definition of ensembles of analogue states. First, we specify a collection of target states densely sampling the full embedding space. For each target state, we search for the ensemble of its k-nearest neighbors, its k-best analogues, and we analyze its volume and dynamics. On the one hand, we study the probability distribution of the volumes and relate its mean and variance to the scale-invariance properties of the stochastic process. On the second hand, we study the Lagrangian properties of the analogues by characterizing how they disperse in time. More particularly, we study the volume occupied by the analogue's successors in function of time and of their initial volume. The main contribution of this paper is to highlight the link between these dynamical properties and the scale-invariance features of the process. We analyze two types of stationary and dissipative 1-dimensional scale-invariant processes: regularized fractional Brownian motion and regularized multifractal random walk. For both processes, the structure and dynamics of the embedding space are determined by their scale-invariant properties.

papers.title: Pseudo-Likelihood Regression for the Marginal Rate of Recurrent Events with a Competing Terminal Event
papers.abstract: Regression modeling of recurrent and terminal events continues to present methodological challenges in survival analysis. Existing approaches either make unverifiable assumptions about the dependence between the two event types, rely on a proportional mean rate assumption, or use ad hoc estimating equations. We propose a semiparametric regression model based on a novel weighted pseudo-likelihood function that directly targets the marginal rate of the recurrent event and extends the Ghosh--Lin model to a large class of transformation models. Our framework accommodates external time-dependent covariate effects on the marginal rate and enables flexible prediction of the marginal mean. We establish consistency and asymptotic normality of the estimators and propose a robust sandwich estimator for the variance. In simulation studies, we demonstrate a strong performance of the proposed estimator under independent right-censoring. We apply the method to data from the interim analysis of a randomized clinical trial on chronic obstructive pulmonary disease to predict the expected number of severe exacerbations, and illustrate how the choice of regression model affects the estimated covariate effects and predictions.

papers.title: Kinetic versus refill-zone uncertainty in predicted pr--burning of methane-oxygen rotating detonation rocket engines
papers.abstract: Rotating detonation rocket engines can lose performance when fresh propellant mixes with hot recirculated combustion products and ignites before the detonation wave arrives. Predicting this pre-burning requires fuel ignition chemistry at high pressure and in product-diluted mixtures, conditions most chemical kinetic mechanisms used in engine simulations were not developed for. With methane as our base fuel, we quantify how strongly predicted pre-burning depends on the choice of mechanism, test the mechanisms against published high-pressure ignition data, and use Bayesian methods to calibrate the most influential uncertain reaction and to assess which measurements would best improve the predictions. As the refill zone is represented by an idealized zero-dimensional model, our results should be viewed as relative comparisons rather than direct engine predictions. Five existing chemical kinetics mechanisms for methane combustion predict refill-zone ignition delays that differ by up to a factor of twenty. Mechanisms without methylperoxy chemistry, including two commonly used in engine simulations, do not reproduce the laboratory data below about 1150 K. Calibrating the CH${_3}$ + HO${_2}$ reaction against these data, while allowing for systematic differences between datasets, increases the relative importance of its chain-terminating channel, consistent with a direct rate measurement. With the data-consistent mechanisms, the remaining kinetic uncertainty in the predicted pre-burnt fraction is, in most cases, several times smaller than the uncertainty arising from the state of the refill zone: the temperature and composition of the recirculated products and the way fresh and burnt gases mix. Improved pre-burning predictions are therefore expected to depend mainly on accurately characterizing the refill zone.

papers.title: Probabilistic framework for infrastructure deformation anomaly warning using InSAR observations
papers.abstract: Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar (InSAR) offers a low-cost, wide-area solution for near continuous infrastructure monitoring. However, translating InSAR observations into automated anomaly warnings remains challenging because displacements are relative, affected by uncertainty, and acquired along line of sight (LOS). This paper introduces a probabilistic warning framework that accounts for these factors. LOS displacements are modelled through a Gaussian distribution. A limit state function is defined to describe the displacement exceedance, and the time-dependent probability of exceedance is evaluated. Instead of a fixed threshold, warnings are identified through abrupt increases in exceedance probability. The framework is tested using three case studies of quay walls in Amsterdam, The Netherlands, providing timely anomaly warnings and issued no warnings for the non-collapse case. Results demonstrate the potential of a probabilistic interpretation of InSAR time series for deformation anomaly warning.

papers.title: Bayesian Image Reconstruction and Uncertainty Quantification for Three-Photon Positronium Ratio Imaging: Toward Radiotheranostic Applications
papers.abstract: Three-photon annihilation imaging can estimate positronium decay ratios with pure positron emitters, including the imaging agents of radiotheranostic pairs, but quantitative reconstruction is limited by heterogeneous localization errors, selection-dependent sensitivity, and background coincidences. We develop a Bayesian reconstruction combining a three-dimensional event-response model with a Poisson likelihood and latent signal-background allocations. Photon-energy and interaction-position uncertainties enter the event covariance; a simulation-calibrated scale mixture accommodates heavy-tailed errors. Posterior sampling gives credible intervals for the three-to-two-photon enhancement ratio. We compare kernel deposition, voxel MLEM, and matched regional maximum likelihood. At 3000 selected events in full-absorption simulation, the regional Bayesian estimator had ratio RMSE 0.067, versus 0.075 for kernel-deposition region-of-interest analysis. In a transport-based four-rod simulation without background, biases averaged at most 3.2% over six independent simulations, whereas background and detector mismatch degraded it. In a measured uniform phantom, the heavy-tailed regional model gave 1.02, 0.74, 1.02 for the 2, 3, 4 mm rods (5 mm reference; nominal 1). Matched regional maximum likelihood agreed with the Bayesian estimates in every simulated setting (bias differences within 0.15 points) and on the measured data (within 0.008), so gains derive from the regional likelihood. Under Poisson Kullback-Leibler loss, Gamma posterior means dominate maximum likelihood, appreciably only at small counts; horseshoe-type and smoothing priors changed voxel images but not regional ratios, whereas shrinking ratios across regions reduced error when regions shared a ratio. Posterior intervals quantify the uncertainty that treatment decisions require; calibration and background modeling remain limiting.

papers.title: Wind Speed Forecasting Using a Spatio-Temporal Hybrid Model: A Case Study of South African Wind Stations
papers.abstract: In this paper, we propose a hybrid forecasting framework that combines temporal ARIMA models and spatial NNGP corrections to improve wind speed predictions at 19 wind stations in South Africa. The proposed framework develops temporal baselines with ARIMA models, applies an NNGP correction to residual spatial dependencies and then combines the two components to produce improved forecasts. RMSE of the hybrid model is reduced by 17.4% (1.416 vs 1.715 m/s) compared to ARIMA baseline (station-wise improvements up to 48.9%); rolling-origin forecast evaluation over five origins with ten-day horizon was used (spatial correlation range = 103km, temporal persistence = 0.46), blockwise conformal prediction intervals cover 99.5% and Diebold-Mariano tests show statistical significance of improvements (DM = 6.44, p < 0.001). Spatial dependencies should be accounted for in temporal forecasting to improve prediction accuracy, especially at high-elevation stations, where spatial effects are strongest.

papers.title: Zero-Shot Prognostic Covariate Adjustment and Mechanistic Week-1 Myelosuppression Updating Across 9,500 Oncology Patients Under FDA Guidance
papers.abstract: The FDA's 2023 guidance on covariate adjustment recommends "that sponsors adjust for covariates that are anticipated to be most strongly associated with the outcome of interest" and notes that "it may be useful to use previous studies (e.g. a Phase 2 trial) to select prognostic covariates or form prognostic indices." Its August 2024 guidance on dosage optimization, part of Project Optimus, states that "the dose- and exposure-response relationships should be evaluated to select a dosage(s) for clinical trial(s)." We analyzed the control arms of 14 randomized trials from Project Data Sphere, with 5,074 patients with overall survival follow-up, in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) and metastatic colorectal cancer (mCRC), and in three AACR Project GENIE Biopharma Collaborative cohorts (4,440 patients). In all, about 9,500 patients were studied. We used the regularized baseline prognostic index to compute out-of-fold estimates of the share of covariate-adjusted log-rank variance removed ($\rho^2$), and found these to be 0.177 to 0.186 for the three indications. For the locked held-out trials, the value was 0.183 (second-line NSCLC docetaxel), 0.177 (first-line PDAC gemcitabine) and 0.110 (first-line mCRC FOLFOX plus bevacizumab). Refitting in GENIE BPC resulted in estimates of 0.073 to 0.127 for first-line and 0.122 to 0.219 for later lines. In a simulated 600-patient trial, 5,000 within-stratum re-randomizations gave a type I error rate of 0.051 for the adjusted test. At $\rho^2 = 0.18$, adjustment raises power from 80.0% to 87.2%, cuts required events by 18% or shrinks the control arm by about 30%. A Friberg marrow prior updated with week 1 blood counts raised the AUROC for new cycle 1 grade 3 or worse neutropenia from 0.791 to 0.816 (n = 3,465; calibration slope 0.999; Brier skill 0.190) and raised it in 5 of 8 cross-trial rows (up to +0.116).

papers.title: Sequential Monitoring of Image Streams Using Energy Statistics
papers.abstract: Sequential monitoring of image data is a high-velocity, high-dimensional big data problem in statistics and machine learning, with wide applications in manufacturing industries, satellite imaging, medical diagnostics, and remote sensing. This is a challenging task because image intensity functions are often contaminated by noise and contain discontinuities and other complicated spatial structures. In the literature, a vast majority of image-monitoring methods rely on changes in image intensity values to detect out-of-control images. However, such approaches are often unreasonable in applications where insignificant changes in image contrast or background intensity should not indicate an out-of-control image as long as the boundaries of the image objects remain unchanged. In this article, we propose a nonparametric Phase II image-monitoring procedure based on energy distance that directly monitors changes in the distribution of image boundaries. The proposed method constructs a moving-window energy-distance-based control statistic by comparing the distribution of recently observed image boundaries with that of a fixed in-control reference sample. The central idea behind the proposed boundary-based approach is twofold: first, to reduce the dimensionality of high-resolution images by retaining relevant edge information, and second, to provide a robust monitoring procedure that is less sensitive to insignificant smooth changes in image intensity. The proposed construction offers a computationally efficient distributional approach to image monitoring without requiring a parametric model for out-of-control images. Theoretical justifications and superior performance in numerical comparisons ensure that the proposed control chart can be useful to many researchers and practitioners.

papers.title: Threshold Generalized Autoregressive Moving Average Models
papers.abstract: Non-Gaussian time series often exhibit nonlinear dynamics and changes in dependence structures that may not be adequately captured by conventional single-regime models. To address this limitation, we introduce a class of threshold generalized autoregressive moving-average (TGARMA) models that combines observation-driven GARMA dynamics with threshold-based regime switching. The proposed framework accommodates multiple regimes, determined by a lagged endogenous or exogenous threshold variable, and allows regression coefficients, autoregressive and moving-average orders and coefficients, and, where applicable, dispersion parameters to vary across regimes. Parameters are estimated by maximum partial likelihood, while model selection is conducted using information criteria. We examine model admissibility and stability, assess model adequacy through residual diagnostics, and conduct a Monte Carlo simulation study to investigate the finite-sample performance of the estimators. The proposed methodology is illustrated using monthly counts of hospitalizations due to respiratory diseases among older adults in S\~ao Paulo, Brazil. In this application, the TGARMA model outperforms its single-regime GARMA counterpart in terms of in-sample mean squared error, highlighting the potential benefits of incorporating regime-dependent dynamics into the analysis of non-Gaussian time series.

papers.title: Fast likelihood evaluation for multivariate sensory discrimination models
papers.abstract: Sensory discrimination is often measured by fitting statistical models with likelihood functions that are computationally challenging to evaluate. In the standard triangle and duo-trio tests, a subject is presented with three stimuli, two of one kind and one of another, and is asked to identify the odd one out (the triangle test) or which of two stimuli matches a reference (the duo-trio test). In a Thurstonian model, the subject's internal representation of each stimulus is a Gaussian whose mean and covariance depend on the stimulus, and the probability that the subject's response is correct is an integral over a $3d$-dimensional Gaussian with no closed form for $d > 1$, where $d$ is the dimension of the stimulus space. To fit a statistical model to data collected from triangle or duo-trio tests, the likelihood function, and often its gradient, need to be evaluated many times, making statistical inference inefficient. Here, we introduce fast algorithms for evaluating certain classes of likelihood functions for the triangle and duo-trio tests. The algorithms rely on reducing the dimension of these functions. The triangle probability, a function of $2d + d(d+1)$ arguments, reduces analytically to a function of $2d$ arguments, and the duo-trio probability, when the two stimuli have equal covariances, reduces to a function of a single scalar for any $d$. After reducing the dimensionality of those functions, we use neural networks and Chebyshev expansions to evaluate the lower-dimensional functions efficiently. Our algorithms demonstrate orders of magnitude speedups over existing approaches at comparable accuracy, both for a single evaluation and when used to compute the maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimate of a model of color discrimination. The dimensionality reduction we use generalizes to non-Gaussian noise models with elliptical level sets, and to tests with more than three stimuli.

papers.title: Why flattening the P-value histogram works: a theory of the standard-deviation optimization in tensor-decomposition-based unsupervised feature extraction
papers.abstract: Background: Tensor-decomposition-based unsupervised feature extraction (TD-based UFE) selects genes by attributing P-values to the components of a gene singular vector under a null normal distribution. The standard deviation sigma of this distribution is unknown and is chosen so that the histogram of the P-values of the genes that are not selected becomes as flat as possible. This heuristic has worked well in practice but has had no theoretical justification. Results: We prove, for a model of signal, mean expression and noise, that the higher-order singular value decomposition has a component that reproduces the experimental design, that the components of its gene singular vector belonging to background genes are approximately normal with standard deviation sigma_0 = sqrt(d)/s, where d is the noise variance and s the singular value, and that signal genes separate from the background even when they form a positive fraction of all genes. We derive the limit of the objective function of the flattening and prove, by a computer-assisted argument based on interval arithmetic, that for 100 histogram bins, Benjamini-Hochberg level 0.01 and every fraction of background genes between 0.1 and 0.99, the limit has a unique minimizer within 1.1% of sigma_0. We formalize the practice of taking the valley to the right of the peak of the objective as a maximum-drop rule and prove that the resulting estimator is consistent up to this bounded bias. Conclusions: Flattening the P-value histogram estimates the noise level of the background genes, with a small and bounded systematic bias, provided that the signals are strong enough to be detected individually and that the noise variances of background genes are nearly equal.

papers.title: Individualized Prediction Bands in Causal Inference with Continuous Treatments
papers.abstract: Individualized treatments are crucial for optimal decision-making and treatment allocation, specifically in personalized medicine based on the estimation of an individual's dose-response curve across a continuum of treatment levels, e.g., drug dosage. Current works focus on conditional mean and median estimates, which are useful but do not provide the full picture. We propose viewing causal inference with a continuous treatment as a covariate shift. This allows us to leverage existing weighted conformal prediction methods with both quantile and point estimates to compute individualized uncertainty quantification for dose-response curves. When used with quantile regression, our method, individualized prediction bands (IPB), enjoys a doubly robust coverage property. We demonstrate IPB via simulations and a real data analysis that assesses the additional medical expenditure caused by continued smoking for selected individuals. Our results show that IPB provides an effective solution to a gap in the individual dose-response uncertainty quantification literature.

papers.title: Vaccine sieve analysis on deep sequencing data using competing risks Cox regression with failure type subject to misclassification
papers.abstract: Understanding how vaccines perform against different pathogen genotypes is crucial for developing effective prevention strategies, particularly for highly genetically diverse pathogens like HIV. Sieve analysis is a statistical framework used to determine whether a vaccine selectively prevents infection by certain genotypes while allowing breakthrough of other genotypes that evade immune responses. Traditionally, these analyses are conducted with a single sequence available per individual acquiring the pathogen. However, modern sequencing technology can provide detailed characterization of intra-individual viral diversity by capturing up to hundreds of pathogen sequences per person. In this work, we introduce methodology that extends sieve analysis to account for intra-individual viral diversity. Our approach estimates vaccine efficacy against viral populations with at least a small threshold of vaccine-mismatched mutations. To account for differential resolution of information from differing sequence counts per person, we use competing risks Cox regression with modeled causes of failure and propose an empirical Bayes approach for the classification model. Simulation studies demonstrate that our approach reduces bias, provides nominal confidence interval coverage, and improves statistical power compared to conventional methods. We apply our method to the HVTN 705 Imbokodo trial, which assessed the efficacy of a heterologous vaccine regimen in preventing HIV-1 infection.

papers.title: Conformal prediction for high-dimensional functional time series: Applications to subnational mortality
papers.abstract: In statistics, forecast uncertainty is often quantified using a specified statistical model, though such approaches may be vulnerable to model misspecification, selection bias, and limited finite-sample validity. While bootstrap procedures may alleviate some of these concerns, their validity is not guaranteed and they are often computationally demanding. Instead, we take a model-agnostic and distribution-free approach, namely conformal prediction, to construct pointwise prediction intervals in high-dimensional functional time series. Among a rich family of conformal prediction methods, we study split, non-conformity score, sequential predictive, and adaptive conformal prediction. In split and non-conformity score conformal prediction, the data are divided into training, validation, and test sets, and the interval width is calibrated on the validation set so that the empirical coverage probability matches the nominal level, by tuning a coefficient of the residual standard deviation and by taking an empirical quantile of the non-conformity scores, respectively. Sequential predictive conformal prediction removes the need for a validation set by updating predictive quantiles sequentially via an autoregressive process, whereas adaptive conformal prediction updates the significance level over time according to the coverage of past intervals. Using subnational age- and sex-specific $\log$ mortality data from Japan and Canada, we compare the finite-sample forecast performance of the conformal prediction methods considered, using empirical coverage probability and the mean interval score.

papers.title: Reconciling Latent Variables and Networks: Exploring and extending the Psychometric-Toolbox
papers.abstract: Since the introduction of network psychometrics, several connections to statistical models in "classical" psychometrics (i.e., Factor Analysis, Structural Equation Modeling, Item Response Theory) as well as to approaches from other research fields have been established. This paper reviews, synthesizes, and extends these developments, presenting them in an accessible visual format. This perspective opens up promising opportunities to extend the psychometric-toolbox by incorporating and learning from statistical methodologies developed in other areas of research, which often address similar or even identical problems. Highlighting these methodological commonalities may also foster collaboration across research fields that have traditionally remained largely independent. Moreover, awareness of these connections may render methodological development more systematic and goal-directed and may enable a meaningful division of labor, for example between the development of statistical methodology and its practical implementation for empirical research through software tools. Finally, these methodological advances provide new opportunities for empirical research and may contribute to a reconciliation with longstanding conceptual issues concerning psychometric constructs and, more broadly, psychological phenomena.

papers.title: A Two Stage Quasi-Likelihood Estimation Method for High Dimensional Generalized Structural Equation Models
papers.abstract: Estimating high dimensional Generalized Structural Equation Models presents severe computational challenges. Traditional simultaneous estimators frequently suffer from numerical instability and prohibitive computational costs. Moreover, there are no tractable algorithms for families such as Poisson, negative binomial, and gamma. To overcome these limitations, this article introduces a Two Stage Quasi-Likelihood Expectation-Maximization framework. The proposed method isolates the structural model from the measurement model. First, it approximates the conditional distribution of the latent variables given the observed indicators. Second, it employs marginal quasi-likelihood estimating equations to evaluate the structural parameters, deriving the necessary conditional moments either exactly or through Monte Carlo integration. This approach completely avoids the need to evaluate the full joint likelihood. Extensive simulations demonstrate that our method drastically reduces computational runtime, providing a numerically stable framework that minimizes the mean squared error and structural bias to yield a scalable and flexible solution for analyzing complex latent variable models.

papers.title: Shortest Path Lengths in Poisson Line Cox Processes: Approximations and Applications
papers.abstract: We study street-constrained ($\ell_1$) shortest paths in a Poisson line Cox process (PLCP), where Poisson points of linear intensity $\mu$ lie on the lines of an underlying Poisson line process (PLP) of density $\lambda$. Under a one-turn restriction, we derive closed-form expressions for the distribution of the nearest-neighbor path length from (i) the typical PLCP point and (ii) the typical PLP intersection, by explicitly evaluating the relevant void probabilities via a geometric decomposition of the feasible path-length set. For the intersection case, we further provide analytically tractable upper and lower bounds that capture the impact of $\lambda$ and $\mu$. Allowing two turns from the typical point, we obtain a computable upper bound using a feasible-set shrinking argument and identify regimes in which it is tight. We also delineate parameter ranges where a one-turn route from a typical intersection can outperform a two-turn route from a typical point. Finally, we discuss how the results enable statistical performance characterization of ride-hailing services in terms of service guarantee, trip time, and consequently, derive dimensioning insights. We also illustrate qualitatively, how the results can be employed to study vehicle-to-vehicle communication broadcast messages near intersections.
